verdicts.why: Describes overuse gone slack with a plain, blunt force and sets it against a neighbour; stays on the gloss, inside the word, and negative is plausible.
Names the overuse and the extra step of writing the thing off as worthless, which is what trite does; both examples are overused expressions and fit this sense.
Places the word as the mildest member of the overuse family and contrasts it with threadbare; still on the gloss and still negative, only gently so.
Names dullness, tiresomeness and the pretension to significance together, exactly the gloss, and the example 'bromidic sermons' fits.
Informal is a register label, and the note keeps both halves of the gloss (dullness and airs) while describing the word's mocking lightness.
Describes the word's dry, clinical force against its heavier twin and keeps the tiresome self-importance the gloss names.
Describes the word's own weight and sound as part of its mockery of dressed-up dullness; on the gloss, inside the word, negative plausible.
Reports hurt in body or mind without degree, matching 'physical or psychological pain', and 'painful slowness' fits as psychological pain.
Low, unbroken, edgeless pain is the dull steady pain of the gloss, the contrast with biting stays inside the word, and 'my aching head' fits.

Informal is a register label and the note keeps the dull steady pain; 'shortened shape' reads as a description of the word's shorter form rather than an origin story, though it sits close to that line.
Correctly reads the gloss as pain shown rather than pain inflicted, and 'agonized screams' fits that outward-facing sense.
British is a permitted register label, and the note restates the expressing-not-inflicting sense of the gloss with identical force.
Describes extreme pain by contrast with aching and by the weight of agony; on the gloss and inside the word.
British spelling is a register fact dictionaries record, and the note keeps the gloss's extremity unsoftened.
Describes the word's force as the ceiling of the extremely-painful set; that is a claim about intensity, not a narrowing of what the gloss covers.
Keeps the extremity of the gloss and distinguishes the word by what the pain costs the sufferer, a difference in force rather than a new sense.
Reads the participle's force as pain done to someone while keeping the gloss's extremity; the contrast with excruciating stays inside the word.
Describes extreme pain as a quality of the experience without an inflicting agent, which fits the gloss and differentiates it from torturing.
